checks_run.req219_new_ac_technical_soundness: PASS -- independently reasoned through real Elixir/OTP Supervisor semantics, not taken on the requirement's own say-so. Supervisor.start_link/2 starts a supervisor's children strictly sequentially and blocks on each child's own init/1 (and, for a child that is itself a Supervisor, its full subtree) completing before starting the next sibling. With the top-level Letflow.Application list as [Infrastructure, Pollers, Http] under :one_for_one: Infrastructure's start_link (and every one of its own children's init/1, including Obs.Alerts.TaskSupervisor, which decision 2 places inside Infrastructure) must return successfully BEFORE the top-level supervisor even calls Pollers.start_link/1, which is what invokes Pollers' own init/1. So under CORRECT order, Process.whereis(Obs.Alerts.TaskSupervisor) is guaranteed non-nil the instant Pollers' init/1 begins executing -- Infrastructure's entire subtree already fully registered by then. Under INCORRECT order ([Pollers, Infrastructure, Http] or any ordering with Pollers first), the top-level supervisor calls Pollers.start_link/1 -- and therefore Pollers' own init/1 -- BEFORE Infrastructure has been started at all, so Obs.Alerts.TaskSupervisor cannot yet be registered and Process.whereis/1 must return nil at that same moment. The two orderings produce genuinely different, mutually exclusive observable outcomes for this exact assertion at this exact moment -- this is not a vacuous check that would pass regardless of order (e.g. it is not merely checking that the process exists SOMETIME after full boot, which would pass under either order once all children eventually start; it is anchored to the moment Pollers' init/1 runs, which is the one point in the startup sequence that order actually controls). The AC's own suggested implementation ('a test child spec or trace hook record the whereis/1 result during Pollers' init') is a real, buildable mechanism -- e.g. instrumenting Pollers.init/1 in a test-only build path, or a :sys/:telemetry trace hook capturing the moment -- so this is testable in practice, not just in principle. No hidden OTP guarantee (e.g. registry pre-population, application start_phases, or eager compilation-time registration) supplies Obs.Alerts.TaskSupervisor's name independently of Infrastructure actually running, since it is only ever registered by being started as one of Infrastructure's own supervised children (per decision 2, already verified against the real 20-child list in my original pass). Conclusion: the new AC's test WOULD distinguish correct from incorrect ordering, not pass vacuously.
